parts.title: Homesteading: A Memoir, Practical Guide, and Policy Analysis

sentences: This book is a **memoir**, a **practical guide**, and a work of **policy and science**.
It recounts building and losing farms over decades, including practical experiences.
The practical guide covers finding and financing a homestead, building **living soil**, keeping chickens, managing livestock, preserving food, and organizing a household and farm.
The policy and science section examines how **food systems** were shaped by agricultural policies, nutritional guidance, and industrial practices.
Health, resilience, and autonomy come from rebuilding the relationship between people, land, and food systems.
The authors are a **scientist, physician, carpenter, farmhand**, animal science major, and have PhDs in biotechnology and public policy.
They are also **farmers, breeders, gardeners**, and cooks, asserting that **health begins in soil**, kitchens, and daily habits.
This conviction was tested over four decades on six farms.
The book is **not medical advice**; health decisions should be made with a **qualified healthcare professional**.
Homesteading and health are **deeply interconnected**.
Homesteading encourages healthy living, and healthy living often leads to homesteading.
Many cope with **food insecurity** by taking responsibility for themselves and their families, aiming for self-sufficiency.
Homesteading involves creating a **stable home**, learning skills like cooking, gardening, food preservation, raising animals, and basic carpentry for **independence and autonomy**.
This lifestyle fosters a deeper connection to the earth.
Homesteading can be done on a **shoestring budget** with skills, thrift, and a willingness to learn.
The journey to becoming competent farmers was also a **journey of self-discovery**.
Ancestral lessons can be rediscovered through practices like growing a **kitchen garden** or raising a few chickens.
Tending even a small piece of land with intention improves **physical and mental health**.
Learning to care for soil organically, without chemicals, is central to the **homesteading ethos**.
Scientific research shows **gardening** is linked to a lower risk of cognitive decline, stronger mental abilities, and longer life.
**Animal husbandry** requires daily responsibility, engaging both body and mind, and contributes to longer life by increasing physical activity, reducing stress, and improving mental well-being.
The authors state that **fear** often prevents people from moving forward, evolving, and building something of their own.

parts.title: Our Journey to Homesteading: The Maryland Farm

sentences: Twenty-five years ago, Robert worked with **Percheron draft horses**, which led them to an **old farm** in **Jefferson, Maryland**.
The farm had **fifty-five acres of rolling hills**, **collapsing barns**, and a **house 100 to 150 years old**.
The house, built by people **without money**, had been rented by a **regional motorcycle gang**.
When bought, it had **no heat**, minimal **electricity**, a **spring box for water**, and a **collapsed bathroom floor**.
A **car jack** supported the bathtub, allowing cold baths, but there was **no hot water** in the kitchen.
They found **used needles**, **syringes**, **ammo**, **lighters**, and **hash pipes**.
A **blacksnake issue** was also present.
The house had **asbestos siding**, but underneath were **chestnut logs**; the upstairs floor sloped **four inches**.
Their teenage children were **not thrilled**, but morale improved with **hot water** and a **functioning bathroom**.

parts.title: Building a Healthy Homestead Through Self-Sufficiency

sentences: Homesteading shifts from **philosophy to practice**, focusing on **building health** through **self-sufficiency**.
It involves finding **land**, organizing a household for **productivity**, choosing **livestock wisely**, growing **nutrient-dense food**, and aligning habits with **long-term resilience**.
This approach emphasizes **steady progress** despite **setbacks**, aiming for **health**, **stability**, and **trusted food**.
The core message is to **cultivate your garden**, which means taking **responsibility** and tending to your **corner of the world**.
Homesteading fosters a transformation from **passive consumer** to **active creator**, bringing focus to **morality**, **independence**, and **free agency**.
**Self-reliance** is crucial for **freedom**, achievable through homesteading, which can be done on a **small or large scale**.
**Creativity** with resources, like using old containers for planting, shows that **expensive setups are not needed**.
Growing your own food, like making **bread with einkorn flour**, offers **nutritional benefits** and a **connection to heritage grains**.
Challenges like **deer** in gardens require **adaptive strategies** like motion-activated lights.
**Time management** in homesteading involves minimizing online entertainment, eating out less, and utilizing **organizational systems** like journals and online calendars.
The goal is to build **healthy families** and **sanctuaries of sanity** through **honest labor** and **community ties**, rather than relying solely on external systems.
Jill's parents were influenced by **World War II**; her father served in the **Royal Air Force**, and her mother raised daughters through the **Blitz**.
Her mother, from **rural stock**, emphasized being a "**good housewife**" through activities like raising chickens and gardening.
Jill's father, a senior engineer, also engaged in **self-sufficiency** by repairing cars and keeping bees.
For their family, **self-sustainability** was simply a way of life.
Robert's family had a parallel story, with his mother influenced by **victory gardens** and **thriftiness**.
A shared love for **land** and **farming** took root when they worked on Jill's father's orchard.
Farming involves **optimism** and requires **dreams**.
Building a homestead involves battling pests like **Japanese beetles** and deer, often deterred by **Australian shepherds**.
The "**back-to-the-earth**" movement of the 1970s influenced them, leading to a plan for Robert to become a **small-town doctor** on a **small farm**.
Their **professional life** financed their homesteading goals.
Finding **financing for land or a farm** is difficult, as conventional loans are not friendly to farm purchases.
They advise **avoiding mortgages** if possible, or opting for **shorter terms**.
**Manufactured homes** can offer good value, especially if purchased with cash.
Upgrading features like windows is wise for quality modular homes, which are cheaper than **stick-built construction**.
Considering **income sources** beyond traditional jobs, such as niche farm products or specialty animal breeding, can provide significant returns.
Breeding registered **mini-Jersey cows** and **white emus** are profitable ventures.
Homesteading requires **resilience**, involving failure and constant adjustment, but it is deeply satisfying.
A **jar** is a **tool** that shifts **control back to the household**.
A shelf full of jars is **visually satisfying**, a **record of work**, and **saved resources**.
It means you are a bit **independent** of the outside world.
**Glass, a lid, and a seal** make a simple tool that makes a big difference.
**Food preservation** requires you to work when food is **ready**, even if it's inconvenient.
Later, opening a jar you filled yourself brings **clarity** to the system.
This is how **effort moves forward in time** and **abundance creates stability**.
It's important to understand what happened to our **food** and how to **fix it**.
This involves **soil depletion**, **nutrient loss**, and the **regenerative path**.
A **supermarket tomato** compared to a **garden tomato** shows a clear difference in **taste**.
Your instincts are right; there is **scientific evidence** explaining why.
The **nutritional quality** of food has declined over **seventy years** due to various causes, which can be addressed on one's **land**.
The story includes **soil chemistry**, **fungal networks**, **industrial farming**, and **hopeful agricultural research**.

parts.title: Companion Planting, Pest Management, and Seed Saving

sentences: **Companion planting** makes a **resilient** and **productive garden**.
The **Three Sisters** method uses **corn**, **beans**, and **squash**.
**Corn** offers a **climb**, **beans fix nitrogen**, and **squash shades**.
**Dill and thyme** **attract beneficial insects** for **cabbage family crops**.
**Lettuce** in **partial shade** improves **yields**.
Avoid **crowding similar crops** and keep **fennel on its own**.
The garden shows problems with **stunted growth** or **pests**.
**Physical barriers** like **row covers** prevent problems.
**Daily observation** is important; **walk the garden**.
**Handpicking insects** works in **smaller gardens**.
**Chickens clean insects**, **guinea fowl control ticks**, and **ducks help in wet environments**.
Start with the **least aggressive option** for intervention.
**Insecticidal soaps**, **neem oil**, and **diatomaceous earth** can **reduce pest loads**.
**Milky spore** is a **slow solution** for **Japanese beetle grubs**, lasting for **years**.
**Beneficial nematodes** are **fast**, **broad-spectrum hunters** for **soil pests**.
**Wood ash** can **deter slugs and snails**.
Only **open-pollinated** or **heirloom varieties** are worth **saving seeds**.
**Beans**, **peas**, and **tomatoes** are easy starting points.
**Saved seeds adapt** to your **soil** and **climate**.
Store seeds **cool**, **dry**, and **out of light**.
**Oats** are a useful winter cover crop that can **winter-kill** in colder temperatures, which means no need to **terminate** them in spring.
They leave a **soft mulch layer** and help **hold soil** through fall and early winter.
**Buckwheat** is a quick summer fix, as it **germinates** in poor soil, grows fast, and **shades out weeds**, also helping to **mobilize phosphorus**.

**Sorghum-Sudangrass** is a summer **biomass king** that grows tall, produces a lot of **organic matter**, and has **deep roots** that improve soil structure, often used for rehabilitating **worn-out ground**.
In the South, **cowpeas** handle heat, **fix nitrogen**, and produce a **usable crop** like black-eyed peas.

In the **South** and lower **Mid-Atlantic**, where winters are mild, **winter rye** with **legumes** like hairy vetch or crimson clover is effective for **soil retention** and **nitrogen fixation**, allowing crops like **collards** to thrive.
Further **north** in the **Midwest** and **Northeast**, winter is harsher, so **rye** is still valuable for cold tolerance, and **oats** are good because they winter-kill and leave **mulch**.
**Daikon radish** is useful for **breaking up compacted soil** and then rotting in place.
In the **Upper Midwest** and **Northern Plains**, simplicity is key due to short growing seasons, so **oats** or **radish** are planted after harvest and terminated by winter.
In the **West**, water is a limiting factor; **sorghum-sudangrass** provides biomass if **irrigation** is available, otherwise **buckwheat** is a scrappy option that tolerates poor conditions.

parts.title: Sheep: Border Collies, Australian Shepherds, and Livestock Management

sentences: **Border collies** are **ideal** for **sheep-only** farms, excelling at **moving flocks** with **quiet intensity**.
They are **not good** at **predator control** and **not livestock guardians**.
You will likely need a **separate guardian breed** for **nighttime predator pressure**.
These dogs **require a job**; without one, they may **herd children**, **guests**, or even **bicycles**.
They **bond deeply** with their owner and prefer to be **involved outdoors**.
If you **don't manage stock regularly**, they might **not be the best fit**.
For **mixed livestock**, especially **cattle**, a **working Australian shepherd** may be **better**.
Some **border collies lose confidence** with **aggressive cattle**, but **working line Australian shepherds** have more **push and grit**.
It's **crucial** to select from **true working stock**, not just **show lines**.
Raising **sheep seriously** involves **training both yourself and your dog**, a process measured in **years**, not **weekends**.
**Clubs**, **trials**, and **lessons** offer chances to **refine timing** and **stock sense**.
This can be a **rewarding pursuit** for those who enjoy **performance events** and **lifelong learning**.
**Sheep** can also serve a **simpler purpose**, grazing quietly for a **storybook scene**.
However, without a **dog**, you will need **extra hands** for **pasture moves** and **health checks**.
**Sheep are cooperative in theory**, but **rarely in practice**.
Consider **breeding for homestead** or **4-H markets**, as **visually distinctive** or **registered animals** fetch **good prices**.
When combined with **meat production**, **wool use**, and **pasture management**, **sheep** can form a **flexible system**.
They are **working livestock** with **multiple revenue streams**, requiring **clear expectations** and **sturdy fencing**.
Always **buy the best you can**, as **low-cost animals** may **cost more in the long term** due to **health issues**.
Australian Shepherds are **excellent farm dogs** and are adept at **herding**, often with a gentle nip to the hocks or heels.
Border Collies also excel with **sheep or poultry** and are **less prone to nipping**.
Both breeds require **ample exercise** and are skilled at learning and **patrolling farm boundaries**.
A lack of activity can lead to **destructive behavior** in these dogs.
A guard dog, like Bella, is essential for a farm, capable of quickly dispatching **groundhogs** and deterring **foxes and other predators**.
Bella also alerts to **strangers** but knows not to attack people, acting as a **threatening alarm system**.
She understands that farm animals are her responsibility, protecting **chickens, poultry, horses, cattle, and emus**.
Bella distinguishes between **livestock and vermin**, knowing that groundhogs dig holes that can injure larger animals or compromise barn foundations.
Mixed herding-breed dogs can also be **effective farm dogs**, but researching a rescue dog's background and consulting a **behaviorist** is recommended.
It is best to **avoid terrier mixes** if you have small livestock or poultry due to their **strong prey drive**.
Livestock Guardian Dogs (LGDs) are an excellent addition for **predator protection**, especially if you lack herding dogs.
LGDs live outside, **bond with livestock**, and require **training and boundaries**.
When selecting an LGD, consider the climate, as many breeds have **heavy coats** that may not suit hot environments.
Homesteading income can come from various sources, including **breeding specialty animals** such as Lusitano horses, which have a niche market and better return on investment than more common breeds.
Careful **selection and breeding** for temperament and athleticism, as practiced with Lusitanos, helps preserve valuable genetic lines and ensures **desirable traits**.
Market trends and **functional genetics** are crucial for successful breeding, as relying solely on show standards can lead to health and behavioral issues.
Breeding for **hardiness and longevity**, like Joel Salatin's approach to chickens, can create more resilient and productive animals for homesteaders.

parts.title: The Art of Intentional Breeding and a Return to Quality

sentences: Returning to **breeding for success** means focusing on **egg production**, **meat quality**, **longevity**, **health**, or **athletic performance**.
We have often **measured the wrong things**, chasing **extreme gaits** and **unusual color patterns** instead of **structural integrity** and **natural fertility**.
Our foundation mare, **Caranja**, imported from Brazil, is the **matriarch** of the farm.
Her **weakness** is **lighter bone** in her legs and **smaller hooves**, but she is considered **modern**, suited for **dressage**.
We knew the market was shifting towards **dressage and sport horses**, making her **lighter bones** more **desirable**.
Our senior stallion, **Jade**, imported from Portugal, stamps his foals with his **steady personality**, **intelligence**, and **calm presence**.
He also passes on his **excellent conformation** and **gaits**, with **more bone** and **large, solid hooves**.
**Quartz CAL**, the son of Caranja and Jade, illustrates a **thoughtful cross**.
He has the **bone and hoof of his sire** and his **sire’s temperament**, combined with the **modern frame** of his **dam**.
Quartz represents the **type of Lusitano** they have been **intentionally breeding toward**.
The goal is to **exhibit Quartz and Topazio together** as a **riding and driving pair** of stallions.
**Lusitano stallions** are typically kept **intact** if they have no **genetic defects** and are often **shown and worked together**.
The **ultimate goal of farming** is not just **growing crops** but the **cultivation and perfection of human beings**.
**Quality animals**, raised with care, will carry their **traits forward for generations**.
**Animal breeding** is an **extraordinary cultural and technological skill** that humans have developed.
It takes **knowledge**, **thought**, **skill**, **resources**, **commitment**, and **time** to do it well.

parts.title: Understanding Full-Fat and Raw Dairy Benefits and Risks

sentences: Full-fat dairy, like **whole milk** and **full-fat cheese**, is linked to a **lower risk of all-cause dementia**.
A study with **7,600 adults** over two decades showed this.
This link **does not necessarily imply causation**.
People who eat **full-fat dairy** may have other good lifestyle habits.
These include **overall diet quality**, **physical activity**, and **socioeconomic factors**.
Dairy fat has many **fatty acids** with different effects.
**Fermented dairy products** add **microbial factors** that can help **gut health**.
**Full-fat dairy** can be part of a **healthy diet**, especially with **minimally processed foods**.
**Whole milk** has **fat-soluble vitamins**, **bioactive lipids**, **proteins and sugars**.
Skimming milk removes much of its fat, changing its **caloric composition**.
**Full-fat dairy** may not raise **cardiovascular disease risk** and could be **beneficial**.
It can be good when it replaces **refined carbohydrates**.
**Whole milk's fat** slows digestion and helps stabilize **blood sugar levels**.
It also reduces hunger, which may prevent **overeating**.
It contains **conjugated linoleic acid (CLA)**, **omega-3s**, and **short- and medium-chain fats** like **butyric acid**.
These support **gut health** and **metabolism**.
**Raw milk** is debated due to its **nutritional** and **microbial characteristics** versus **infectious disease** risk.
**Pasteurization** greatly reduced milk-borne illnesses like those from **Mycobacterium bovis**.
Interest in raw milk continues for those wanting **less processed foods**.
Studies in **farm environments** link **raw or minimally processed milk** to less **asthma** and **allergic disease**.
This is the **“farm milk effect”**, where kids exposed to **unprocessed farm milk** show lower rates of **respiratory and allergic conditions**.
**Raw milk** has **heat-sensitive bioactive components** like **immunoglobulins** that help **immune system development**.
**Bacterial infection** risk is higher with **raw milk** than pasteurized milk.
The absolute risk for individuals is **relatively low**.
But there can be severe outcomes for vulnerable people.
The **risk of illness** from properly handled raw milk is **low at the individual level**.

parts.title: The Transformation of American Agriculture Under Earl Butz

sentences: Secretary of Agriculture Earl Butz promoted **efficiency**, **scale**, and **productivity** in farming, encapsulated by his phrase, “**get big or get out**.”

This approach encouraged **consolidation**, **mechanization**, and **high-output commodity production**, with **subsidy structures** and **research priorities** aligning to support larger operations and higher yields.

These policies significantly increased **agricultural productivity**, making the United States a leading producer of **corn**, **soybeans**, and **wheat**, but also led to a decline in **small farms** and concentrated agricultural production, affecting **rural communities**.

The long-term effects are still debated, with increased efficiency stabilizing **food supply** and reducing costs, yet raising concerns about **environmental sustainability**, **soil health**, **biodiversity**, and the **resilience** of highly centralized systems.

The current agricultural landscape is shaped by these **policy choices**, not solely by **market forces**, providing context for homesteaders and small-scale farmers to understand or challenge existing systems.

The shift to **large-scale industrial production** under Butz accelerated the decline of the **traditional family farm** and strengthened **agribusinesses**, with economic, environmental, and social consequences that still affect **rural life**.
Many **small towns weakened** as families left farms, leading to **mounting debt**, **volatile commodity prices**, and shrinking **profit margins** for those who remained.
Farming became more **capital-intensive**, requiring **scale** for success, as highlighted by Butz's own words: “**Fewer farmers meant more factory workers**” and “**Get big or get out**.”
This structural transformation benefited **large-scale factory farms**, **agribusinesses**, and **financiers**, while **small, diversified farmers** struggled to compete.
The aim was to boost **productivity**, drive down costs, and maximize yields to “**feed the world**” by producing more food at lower prices.

Butz believed in dismantling New Deal-era supply controls to allow **market forces** to determine prices, aiming for a more **self-sufficient agriculture** less reliant on government payments, though **subsidies continued** and increasingly favored **large operations**.

parts.title: The Influence of Industry on Dietary Guidelines and the Health Risks of Glyphosate

sentences: A **2016 historical analysis** in **JAMA Internal Medicine** highlighted that saturated fat and dietary cholesterol were considered the main causes of **coronary heart disease**, overlooking sugar's role in **cardiovascular risk** through **triglycerides** and **metabolism**.
This framing supported the **lipid hypothesis**, directing research to reduce **fat** rather than focusing on **refined carbohydrates** and **added sugars**.
The **public health impact** was significant, as national dietary guidelines promoted **low-fat eating habits**.
Food companies reformulated products, replacing fat with **refined carbohydrates** and **added sugars**.
The scientific narrative that **minimized sugar's risks** allowed **high sugar consumption** to continue with little scrutiny.
Over time, evidence linked excessive **added sugar intake** to **insulin resistance**, **type 2 diabetes**, **nonalcoholic fatty liver disease**, and **cardiometabolic dysfunction**.
The incident also **eroded public trust** in **nutrition science** when **undisclosed funding** was revealed, showing how **financial sponsorship** can influence research and **public health**.
**Glyphosate**, the most widely used **herbicide**, was initially considered safe due to its mechanism blocking a biological pathway in plants but not animal cells.
However, the **International Agency for Research on Cancer** classified it as a **probable human carcinogen** in **2015**, a classification highly contested by **industry lobbyists**.

Recent research, including a **2023 NCI-funded study**, found that farmers with higher **glyphosate exposure** had elevated markers of **oxidative damage to DNA** and **cell membranes**, providing a plausible mechanism for **cancer promotion**.

The **Global Glyphosate Study (2025)** exposed rats to doses considered safe by EU regulators, and these rats developed **more tumors** in various organs, including **leukemia**, **skin tumors**, and **adrenal cortex cancer**.
**Non-Hodgkin lymphoma** is consistently linked to glyphosate in human studies, with a **2021 review** providing **ample evidence for an association**.
Other studies point to **kidney cancer** and **breast cancer** as areas of concern, suggesting **endocrine-disrupting properties**.

parts.title: Homesteading: Personal Solutions, Not Systemic Fixes

sentences: Homesteading is not a **solution** for the structural problems of the industrial food system, like **subsidy structures** that favor commodity monoculture or the political power of **agribusiness**.
These issues need **political action**.
Homesteading **resolves personal exposure** to the worst industrial products, meaning you can eat **more nutrient-dense food** if you grow your own vegetables in **living soil** without chemicals.

Raising your own chickens or buying eggs from a **known farmer** provides nutritionally superior eggs, and consuming fresh milk from a dairy animal on good pasture offers a product **biologically different** from processed commodity milk.
Eliminating ultra-processed foods **reduces exposure** to glyphosate residues, industrial seed oils, added sugars, and synthetic food dyes, which **contribute to the metabolic crisis**.
These are not trivial **outcomes**.
Homesteading also gives a sense of **agency** by knowing what is in your food and how it was produced, which is not available in the modern food system.
When you grow your own food, you know **exactly what went into your soil** and what your animals ate.
This knowledge **changes everything**, affecting not just what you eat but how you think about the **connection between choices and health**.
Self-sufficiency is a **continuous journey**, not a destination, as total independence is impossible and undesirable.
The goal is to **produce more**, buy more **deliberately**, reduce health-consequential **dependencies**, and build **household competence**.
